sections.title: Pain prevention and management during procedures

read.text: Introduction:

This chapter encompasses a range of interventions and procedures that are important for emergency and ongoing care of neonate at. Mastery of these skills by healthcare professionals is essential to provide timely, effective, and safe care to neonates, ultimately improving neonatal outcomes and reducing the burden of neonatal morbidity and mortality.
This chapter aims to

• Standardize neonatal care practices
  • Enhance the competency of healthcare personnel
  • Ultimately improve neonatal outcomes.
PRACTISE THIS SKILL Procedure Documentation

It is important that the physician performing the procedure document the informed consent process. Include the date, time, additional providers present (if applicable), brief summary of the consent conversation, the diagnosis, recommended procedure, specific risks and benefits, and alternative treatments.
It is equally important to document if a patient refuses a procedure and that the risks associated with refusal were discussed.
Risks of procedures

• 1. All invasive procedures involve pain, risk for infection and bleeding, and potential injury to neighboring structures.
  • 2. Sedation and analgesia should be planned, and the risks of such explained to the parent and/or patient as appropriate.
  • 3. Universal precautions and proper sterile technique should be followed for all patient contact that exposes the healthcare provider to bodily fluids.
What must the physician document before an invasive procedure?
options: The informed consent process: date, time, who was present, the conversation, diagnosis, procedure, risks, benefits and alternatives
Nothing if the baby is very sick
read.explanation: A refusal, and the risks of refusing that were discussed, are documented too.

read.text: 7.1 Procedure Pain prevention and management

sections.title: Pain prevention: environmental and behavioural approaches

read.text: Environmental and behavioral approaches during procedure

• Clustering painful interventions prior to a comforting events (e.g. feeding or holding)
  • Swaddling (tightly wrapping with cloth) during the procedure
  • Non-nutritive sucking: pacifier
  • Change diaper
Following the procedure

• Reducing noise and light
  • Touch or massage
  • Skin to skin contact (Kangaroo Mother Care)
  • Holding the baby using blanket rolls
Physiological interventions
Glucose analgesia: -

• 25 % - 30% sucrose ( glucose) 1.5 – 3 ml PO ~ 2 minutes prior to the procedure for term newborns
  • 25 % sucrose (glucose) 0.5 – 1.5 ml PO ~2 minutes prior to the procedure for preterm NB
  • Suckling a nipple used as analgesia for peripheral venous punctures.
Competitive stimulation
• Gentile rubbing, taping or vibrating one extremity before and during painful stimulus to another extremity
How much 25% sucrose is given to a preterm newborn before a painful procedure, and when?
options: 0.5–1.5 ml by mouth about 2 minutes before
None: sucrose is only for term babies
read.explanation: Term newborns: 25–30% sucrose 1.5–3 ml about 2 minutes before. Add swaddling, non-nutritive sucking, and skin-to-skin after.

read.title: Preventing pain during procedures
read.caption: Clustering care, swaddling, non-nutritive sucking, oral sucrose 2 minutes before a heel prick, and skin-to-skin after.

sections.title: Umbilical artery and umbilical vein catheterization

read.text:
• Indications: blood pressure, monitoring (via umbilical artery [UA]), or blood gas monitoring (via UA) in critically ill neonates
  • Complications: Infection; bleeding; perforation of vessel; thrombosis with distal embolization, schemia or infarction of lower extremities, bowel, or kidney; arrhythmia if catheter is in the heart; air embolus
  • Contraindications: Omphalitis, peritonitis, possible/confirmed necrotizing enterocolitis, intestinal hypo perfusion.
  • Equipment and supplies
      • High-level disinfected or sterile umbilical catheter or ordinary gastric tube:
          • If the baby weighs less than 1.5 kg, use a 3.5-F catheter
          • If the baby weighs 1.5 kg or more, use a 5-F catheter
      • Sterile infusion set with IV fluid (use a micro dropper if one is available)
      • Sterile 5 or 10 ml syringe
      • Sterile drapes
      • Sterile blade
      • Cord tie or suture (to control bleeding)
      • Sterile forceps
      • Sterile suture, adhesive strapping, or thin paper tape (to secure catheter)
  • Line placement :
      • Low line: Tip of catheter should lie just above the aortic Bifurcation between L3 and L4.
      • High line: Tip of catheter should be above the diaphragm between T6 and T9. A high line has fewer complications and lesser need for replacement than a low line.
  • Catheter length: Determine the length of catheter required using following birth weight (BW) regression formula: UAC high line (cm) = (3 x BW [kg]) t 9
PRACTISE THIS SKILL Procedure for UAC line

• Determine the length of the catheter to be inserted for either high (T6 to T9) or low (L3 to L4) position.
  • Restrain infant. Maintain the infant’s temperature during the procedure. Prepare and drape the umbilical cord and adjacent skin using sterile technique.
  • Flush the catheter with sterile saline solution before insertion. Ensure that there are no air bubbles in the catheter or attached syringe.
  • Tie sterile umbilical tape around the base of the cord, tight enough to prevent bleeding. Cut through the cord horizontally about 1.5 to 2 cm from the skin.
  • Identify the one large, thin-walled UV and two smaller, thick-walled arteries. Use one tip of open, curved forceps to gently probe and
  • Dilate one artery. Then use both points of closed forceps and dilate artery by allowing forceps to open gently.
  • Grasp the catheter 1 cm from its tip with toothless forceps and insert the catheter into the lumen of the artery. Aim the tip toward the feet and gently advance the catheter to the desired distance. Do not force.
  • If resistance is encountered, try loosening umbilical tape, applying steady and gentle pressure, or manipulating the angle of the umbilical cord to the skin. Often the catheter cannot be advanced because of the creation of a “false luminal tract.”
There should be good blood return when the catheter enters the iliac artery.

• Confirm catheter tip position with x-ray or ultrasound. Secure catheter with a suture through the cord, a marker tape, and a tape bridge. The catheter may be pulled back but not advanced once the sterile field is broken.
  • Observe for complications: Blanching or cyanosis of lower extremities, perforation, thrombosis, embolism, or infection. If any complications occur, the catheter should be removed.
  • Use isotonic fluids containing heparin per institutional policy. Never use hypoosmolar fluids in the UA.

read.question: A baby weighs 2 kg. Using the manual's formula, how long is the UAC high line?
read.explanation: UAC high line (cm) = (3 × BW in kg) + 9 = 3 × 2 + 9 = 15 cm. The high line tip lies between T6 and T9.

read.title: Umbilical artery catheterization
read.caption: Measuring, preparing the cord, identifying the two arteries and the vein, dilating an artery, advancing the catheter, confirming the tip by X-ray, securing.

read.text:
• Indications: Vascular access when the need for IV access is urgent but a peripheral IV line cannot be established quickly.
      • All babies <1000 g
      • all preterm infants with a gestational age of equal or less than 28 weeks
      • Neonatal with mechanically ventilation or with FiO2 of greater than 40% on continuous positive airway pressure.
      • Exchange transfusion.
      • Hemodynamic instability
      • Administration of hypertonic solutions (e.g. glucose >12.5%, parenteral nutrition or inotropes)
  • Contraindications:
      • Omphalitis
      • Peritonitis
      • possible/confirmed necrotizing enterocolitis
      • intestinal hypoperfusion
      • Umbilical sepsis
  • Complications:
      • Infection
      • Bleeding
      • perforation of vessel
      • thrombosis with distal embolization
      • ischemia or infarction of lower extremities, bowel, or kidney
      • arrhythmia if catheter is in the heart; air embolism.
  • Equipment and supplies
      • High-level disinfected or sterile umbilical catheter or ordinary gastric tube:
          • If the baby weighs less than 1.5 kg, use a 3.5-F catheter
          • If the baby weighs 1.5 kg or more, use a 5-F catheter
      • Sterile infusion set with IV fluid (use a micro dropper if one is available)
      • Sterile 5- or 10-ml syringe
      • Sterile drapes
      • Sterile blade
      • Cord tie or suture (to control bleeding)
      • Sterile forceps
      • Sterile suture, adhesive strapping, or thin paper tape (to secure catheter)
  • Preparation :
      • Determine Umbilical venous catheter (UVC) site: lines should be placed in the inferior vena cava above the level of the ductus venosus and the hepatic veins and below the level of the right atrium.
      • Determine Catheter length:
          • Determine the length of catheter required using either a standardized graph based on shoulder-umbilical length or
          • use distance between xiphisternum and umbilicus +1, plus stump, or
          • The following birth weight (BW) regression formula:
          • 1. UAC high line (cm) = (3 x BW [kg]) + 9
          • 2. UVC length (cm) = 0.5 x UAC high line (cm) + 1
PRACTISE THIS SKILL Procedure for UVC line

• Determine the length of the catheter to be inserted
  • Restrain infants. Maintain the infant’s temperature during the procedure. Prepare and drape the umbilical cord and adjacent skin using sterile technique.
  • Flush the catheter with sterile saline solution before insertion. Ensure that there are no air bubbles in the catheter or attached syringe.
  • Tie sterile umbilical tape around the base of the cord, tight enough to prevent bleeding. Cut through the cord horizontally about 1.5 to 2 cm from the skin.
  • Isolate the thin-walled UV, clear thrombi with forceps, and insert catheter, aiming the tip toward the right shoulder. Gently advance the catheter to the desired distance. Do not force. If resistance is encountered, try loosening the umbilical tape, applying steady and gentle pressure, or manipulating the angle of the umbilical cord to the skin. Resistance is commonly met at the abdominal wall and again at the portal system. Do not infuse anything into the liver.
  • As the catheter is advanced, periodically apply gentle suction with the syringe until blood flows back. Once blood flows back freely through the catheter (usually after the catheter is inserted 5 to 7 cm), do not advance the catheter any further.
  • If resistance is encountered while advancing the catheter, especially in the first 2 to 3 cm, do not continue. Remove the catheter and try again.
  • Tie the cord tie or suture around the stump of the umbilicus to hold the catheter in place and prevent bleeding around the catheter or from one of the arteries.
  • Remove the syringe and connect the infusion set to the catheter, ensuring that there are no air bubbles in the set.
  • Secure the catheter with suture material or adhesive tape to prevent it from being dislodged.
  • Confirm catheter tip position with x-ray or ultrasound.
  • The catheter may be pulled back but not advanced once the sterile field is broken.
  • Look for redness and swelling around the umbilicus, which may indicate infection. If redness or swelling is seen at any time, stop the infusion and remove the umbilical vein catheter. Attempt to establish a peripheral IV line again, and treat for infection of the umbilicus

read.question: For the same 2 kg baby (UAC high line 15 cm), how long is the UVC?
read.explanation: UVC length (cm) = 0.5 × UAC high line + 1 = 0.5 × 15 + 1 = 8.5 cm.

read.text: Which of these is a contraindication to umbilical vein catheterization?
read.explanation: The other three are indications in the manual. Contraindications: omphalitis, peritonitis, possible or confirmed NEC, intestinal hypoperfusion, umbilical sepsis.

read.title: Umbilical vein catheterization (UVC)
read.caption: Isolating the thin-walled vein, advancing until blood flows back freely, securing, connecting the infusion without air, confirming the tip position.

read.text: Indications.

• When intravenous access is anticipated for an extended period. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends placing PICC access if therapy is needed for >6 days.
  • High-risk patient populations (surgical).
  • In low birthweight infants when it is anticipated that full enteral feedings will not be achieved within a short period.
  • Fluid delivery, nutritional solutions, and medications when other venous access is not acceptable or able to be obtained (eg, hypertonic intravenous [IV] solutions).
  • Common sites of PICC line insertion
  • There are multiple potential sites for PICC line insertion.
  • The most commonly used are the antecubital and basilic veins in the upper limbs and the long saphenous veins in the lower limbs.
  • Axillary and scalp veins may also be used.
  • The operator should take time to identify the most suitable point for venous cannulation
  • A number of suitable veins lie in close proximity to arteries risking inadvertent cannulation of an artery. See later section – Specific risks of malposition
Preparation:

• Examine the infant to identify a suitable vein
  • Measure the maximum insertion distance
      • Upper limbs/ head & neck: Measure from the likely entry point to the supra-sternal notch.
      • Lower limbs: Measure from the entry site to the umbilicus
  • If perfusion is poor it may be necessary to correct this prior to line insertion.
  • It is appropriate to correct any significant coagulopathy before commencing the procedure however there is no requirement to routinely check FBC and coagulation profile if there is no evidence of a bleeding tendency.
      • Consider platelet transfusion before the line is placed, particularly if the Platelet count is <50 or there is evidence of excess bleeding from venipuncture sites
  • If the infant is known, or strongly suspected to be septic, it may be wise to delay the placement of a PICC line until the sepsis is under control. PICC lines may easily become colonized with micro-organisms which may then prove difficult to eradicate whilst the line remains in situ.
  • Where possible veins suitable for PICC lines (e.g. saphenous vein) should not be used for peripheral cannulation and venesection in the first few days to leave them available for this purpose.
Placing PICC

• PICC line placement should be performed, or directly supervised, by an operator experienced in their insertion
  • Full aseptic precautions must be observed. A gown and sterile gloves must be worn and a surgical (hernia) towel used
  • Use the drapes to cover the infant from head to toe
  • The line should be flushed with 0.9% sodium chloride for injection prior to placement and the clamp closed. This will help prevent occlusion whilst awaiting an X-ray. Use a 10ml syringe
  • Sterilise the skin around the insertion site according to standard sterile technique. Allow the sterilising solution to dry completely before commencing insertion. Contact with antiseptic solutions may weaken the lines and cause premature failure. If there is any residual antiseptic solution pooling around the limb this should be cleaned off with a saline soaked swab before the procedure.
  • Insert the introducer until flashback is noted or free-flowing blood is obtained
  • Insert the long line and use non-toothed forceps to gently advance the line
  • Do not insert the line further than the optimum insertion distance measured before the procedure
  • If the line will not advance to the measured distance, the tip may have entered the start of an adjoining vessel. Attempts can be made to bypass this by withdrawing the line and then attempting further advancement. Do not leave the tip sitting against such an obstruction.
  • Once successfully inserted, remove the introducer and apply gentle pressure to the insertion site until all oozing of blood around the PICC line has stopped
  • Secure the line in place with a steristrip close to the entry site then cover the line with a Tegaderm dressing (or similar semi-permeable clear dressing) ensuring that all of the polyurethane part of the catheter is covered. This will involve looping the redundant portion around the entry site NB Ensure the junction between the polyurethane part of the catheter and the wider bore section is covered by the dressing as this is a site which is prone to snapping if not supported
When does the CDC recommend PICC access?
options: When therapy is needed for more than 6 days
read.explanation: Upper limb insertions are measured to the suprasternal notch; lower limb insertions to the umbilicus.

read.title: Inserting a PICC line
read.caption: Measuring the insertion distance, full aseptic technique, introducer, advancing with non-toothed forceps, securing with steristrip and transparent dressing.

read.text: Indications: Establishing intravenous access in a newborn baby can be difficult. In an emergency, a good temporary alternative is the intraosseous route using the bone marrow cavity. Fluid and drugs can be given by this route. Remove the intraosseous line as soon as other IV access is established (within eight hours, if possible).
Contraindication: Do not place an intraosseous line if there is infection at the intended insertion site or if the bone is fractured
Complications:

• Extravasation of fluid from incomplete or through-and-through cortex penetration
  • Infection
  • Bleeding
  • Osteomyelitis
  • compartment syndrome
  • fat embolism
  • Fracture
  • epiphyseal injury
Preparation: Determine Sites of entry (in order of preference):

• Anteromedial surface of the proximal tibia, 1 to 2 cm below and slightly medial to the tibial tuberosity on the flat part of the bone
      • Distal femur 3 cm above the lateral condyle in the midline
      • Medial surface of the distal tibia 1 to 2 cm above the medial malleolus (may be a more effective site in older children than the distal femur)
      • Proximal humerus, 2 cm below the acromion process into the greater tubercle with the arm held in adduction and internal rotation
      • Anterior Superior iliac spine at a 90-degree angle to the long axis of the Body
  • Prepare the solution to be infused, ensuring that the entire infusion set is filled with fluid and that there is no air in the infusion set.
  • Prepare the skin over the insertion site using a swab or cotton-wool ball soaked in antiseptic solution, and allow it to dry.
PRACTISE THIS SKILL Procedure:

• Prepare the selected site in a sterile fashion.
  • If the child is conscious, anesthetize the puncture site down to the periosteum with 1% lidocaine (optional in emergent situations).
  • Position the baby’s leg with the knee bent about 30 degrees and the heel resting on the table. Support the upper tibia with one hand, placed so that the hand is not directly behind the site insertion.
  • Insert an 18-gauge (for infants and neonates) IO needle perpendicular to the skin at an angle away from the epiphyseal plate, and advance to the periosteum. With a boring rotary motion, penetrate through the cortex until there is a decrease in resistance, indicating that you have reached the marrow. The needle should stand firmly without support. Secure the needle carefully.
  • attempt to aspirate marrow. (Note that it is not necessary to aspirate marrow.) Flush with crystalloid solution. Observe fluid extravasation. Marrow can be sent to determine glucose levels, chemistries, blood types and crossmatches, hemoglobin levels, blood gas analyses, and cultures.
  • slowly inject 3 ml of IV fluid to check for proper placement of needle
  • Look for swelling (indicating leaking of fluid under the skin) at the front of the leg or in the calf muscle at the back of the leg. If swelling is seen, remove the needle and try again;
  • If it is difficult to infuse the fluid but there is no swelling in the calf muscle, the needle may have entered the posterior bone cortex. Withdraw the needle approximately 0.5 cm and cautiously inject IV fluid again.
  • If no problems are detected, Secure the IO needle. Attach standard IV tubing.
Increased pressure (through pressure bag or push) may be necessary for infusion.
There is a high risk for obstruction if continuous high-pressure fluids are not flushed through the IO needle.
• Remove the intraosseous needle as soon as alternative IV access is available, and within eight hours, if possible.
Where is the first-choice site for intraosseous access in a newborn?
options: The anteromedial proximal tibia, 1–2 cm below and slightly medial to the tibial tuberosity
read.explanation: Remove the IO line as soon as other IV access is established, within eight hours if possible.

read.title: Intraosseous access
read.caption: Positioning the leg, inserting an 18-gauge IO needle with a rotary motion, checking with 3 ml of fluid, looking for swelling, securing.

read.text: Indications for intubation Neonatal tracheal intubation is required during the golden hour for a number of reasons, including

• 1. airway management,
  • 2. surfactant administration and
  • 3. assisting ventilation in respiratory insufficiency.
PRACTISE THIS SKILL Steps of intubation
Here is a summary of the steps for intubation according to NRP:

• 1. Assessment: Assess the need for intubation based on the newborn's clinical condition and response to initial resuscitation measures.
  • 2. Gather equipment: Ensure all necessary equipment for intubation, including a laryngoscope, endotracheal tube, suction, and securing devices, is readily available and prepared.
  • 3. The intubation set for emergency intubation in the delivery room should always be ready and checked before receiving the baby.
  • 4. For equipment preparation, see the setup equipment in the mechanical ventilation section
LARYNGOSCOPY & ET TUBE INSERTION

• 1. Holding the laryngoscope in the left hand, use the right hand to open the mouth wide (premedication can cause some spasm that may need to be overcome)
  • 2. Gently insert the blade to push the tongue to the left and advance towards the throat
  • 3. Use the uvula to help maintain position in the midline. If the uvula is not in the midline, reposition the scope is usually heading to the left
  • 4. Advance the blade forward gently Lift the laryngoscope handle in a forward and upward motion
Avoid a levering action against the top gum

• 5. Instructors' hands on the infant's neck can feel the blade tip (to help guide if the scope is too far in or not far enough)
  • 6. Cricoid pressure can be applied using the little finger of the left hand, or by an assistant (care should be taken not to exert excessive pressure)

(With the video laryngoscope, an airway assistant may also lift the top lip of the infant to allow more space if obtaining a direct airway view and to allow more space for insertion of the ET tube in the mouth.

• 7. Use suction only if secretions are impairing the view
  • 8. Bring the posterior larynx and vocal cords into view, as shown below:
  • 9. Hold the tube high up and with the natural slope facing forward, as it is easier to direct
  • 10. Feed the tube in from the side to allow visualisation of it passing through the cords
  • 11. Use the black marker near the tip of the tube as a guide to the depth of insertion initially
  • 12. Adjust to the previously measured naso-tragal +1cm measurement
  • 13. Be cautious as to how far to insert the tube, as it is often too far in.
  • 14. Secure the ETT tube against the roof of the palate or firmly at the lips
  • 15. Carefully remove the laryngoscope and introducer (if used)
  • 16. Confirm ETT position: chest rise, auscultate for air entry, and connect the CO2 detector and ventilation circuit to confirm correct ETT position.
  • 17. Secure ET with an appropriate fixation device, ensuring a good seal to the skin and avoiding traction on the ETT
  • 18. Provide IPPV once the ET position is confirmed and throughout the securing process
  • 19. Attach the ETT to the ventilator and adjust settings as required
  • 20. Move the infant back into position carefully, ensuring ET is secure when moving the infant and using a 2-person technique to avoid accidental extubation

Post-intubation care: Continuously monitor the newborn's vital signs, oxygenation, and ventilation after successful intubation. It's important to note that intubation is an advanced procedure that should be performed by trained healthcare providers with expertise in neonatal airway management and in accordance with NRP guidelines and protocols.
Post-intubation procedure

• 1. Chest x-ray is the gold standard in confirming the correct ETT position; the ET tip should be visible 1cm above carina (T2-T3)
  • 2. Consider shortening the ETT to minimise dead space
  • 3. Ensure blades are sent for sterilisation as per unit protocol
  • 4. Ensure accurate documentation of the procedure, including the position of the ETT on chest x-ray and whether or not adjustments were made
  • 5. Update parents
What is the gold standard to confirm the ETT position, and where should the tip be?
options: Chest X-ray; tip 1 cm above the carina (T2–T3)
Saturation only; anywhere in the trachea
CO₂ detector only; at the vocal cords
read.explanation: At the bedside: chest rise, air entry on auscultation and a CO₂ detector.

read.title: Endotracheal intubation of a newborn
read.caption: Laryngoscope in the left hand, blade pushing the tongue left, lifting forward and up, tube passed through the cords from the side, depth by the naso-tragal measurement + 1 cm, confirmation.

read.text: Indications: Evacuation of a tension pneumothorax
Complications: Infection; bleeding; pneumothorax; hemothorax; pulmonary contusion or laceration; puncture of diaphragm, spleen, or liver; or bronchopleural fistula
PRACTISE THIS SKILL Procedure:

• a. Prepare and drape the skin as clean as possible, with goal of sterility.
  • b. Insert a large-bore angio-catheter (14- to 22-gauge, based on patient size and likely depth of the chest wall) into the anterior second intercostal space in the midclavicular line. Insert needle over superior aspect of rib margin to avoid neurovascular structures. If the angiocatheter permits, a 3- to 10-mL syringe with 1 to 2 mL of saline can be connected to it. Aspirating the syringe while inserting the IV will pull air bubbles through the saline if an air collection exists. A rush of bubbles signifies successful access.
  • c. When pleural space is entered, withdraw needle and attach a threeway stopcock and syringe to the catheter, and aspirate air. The stopcock is used to stop air flow through the catheter when sufficient evacuation has been performed.
  • d. Subsequent insertion of a chest tube is necessary for ongoing release of air. It is advised not to completely evacuate chest prior to placement of chest tube to avoid pleural injury.
Where is a needle inserted to relieve a tension pneumothorax?
options: The anterior second intercostal space, midclavicular line, over the top of the rib
The fourth space, left sternal edge
read.explanation: Over the superior aspect of the rib margin avoids the neurovascular bundle. A chest tube follows for ongoing air release.

read.title: Needle thoracotomy for tension pneumothorax
read.caption: Landmarks, angiocatheter with a saline-filled syringe, bubbles on entry, three-way stopcock and aspiration.

read.text: Chest tube placement, or thoracostomy, is a critical procedure performed to drain air, fluid, or pus from the pleural space. Indications in the neonate are similar to those in adults. However, the anatomical differences between these populations make neonatal thoracostomy tube placement challenging to the untrained provider.
Objectives:

• To Identify the signs and symptoms indicating that a neonate needs chest tube placement.
  • To Implement proper techniques when performing chest tube placement in the neonate.
  • To Identify chest tube placement complications.
  • Collaborate with other healthcare professionals to enhance health outcomes by providing efficient, comprehensive, and coordinated care to neonates requiring a thoracostomy and post-procedure care.
Indications
Chest tube placement has multiple indications in the neonatal population.

• to remove air
  • to remove fluids, pus, chyle, blood from the pleural space
  • The chest tube is less commonly used to direct fluids or medications into the pleural space
  • chest tube placement is usually indicated following emergent needle decompression.
Contraindications chest tube placement has no absolute contraindications in the neonate. However,
relative contraindications include the presence of;

• diaphragmatic hernias
  • systemic anti-coagulation,
  • Special precautions should be undertaken for neonatal patients following cardiac or thoracic surgery, given their unique thoracic anatomy.
Equipment
The clinician should become familiar with supplies included in chest tube kits at their institution, as instruments included in these kits vary:

• Chest tube: 10F to 12F for infants weighing greater than 1500 grams; 8F to 10F for infants weighing less than 1500 grams
  • Atrium, sealed, or Pleur-evac® drainage system [16]
  • Sterile procedure attire, including gowns, gloves, and hats
  • Sterile prep and drapes to ensure a sterile field
  • Scalpel for skin incision, either a 15-blade or 11-blade
  • Clamp for blunt dissection and pleural entry, either a curved Kelly clamp or mosquito hemostat
  • 4-0 (or 3-0) silk suture on cutting needle
  • Occlusive dressing (Tegaderm, xeroform, 4 x 4 gauze)
Which chest tube size does the manual give for a baby under 1500 g?
read.explanation: 10F to 12F for infants over 1500 g.

sections.title: Chest tube insertion: personnel and steps

read.text: Personnel:

Only authorized individuals properly trained in placing a chest tube should perform the procedure. An assigned assistant may be present to aid the provider performing the chest tube placement. Depending on the patient's size and age, sedation and analgesia most likely will need to be provided by another physician to ensure limited movement and patient discomfort during the procedure. For neonates and children, the presence of another physician or specialist may be required to ensure that the airway is secure and the patient’s vital signs are properly monitored during chest tube placement. In most small neonates and infants, general anesthesia with endotracheal intubation may be preferred.
Preparation
The patient's vital signs should be carefully monitored to ensure no further clinical compromise occurs, especially if the patient is already has symptoms from the pleural fluid or air.

Additionally, a local anesthetic may be injected to minimize procedural discomfort, Administering local anesthetic agents directly under the skin by creating a wheal and in the projected track of the deeper dissection down to the rib can provide additional pain relief.

Sterile tools, including sterile towels, gloves, hats, masks, gowns, and equipment. The area of incision will require adequate skin cleansing using surgical antimicrobial skin swabs (eg, Betadine or chlorhexidine).
PRACTISE THIS SKILL Technique of insertion:

• Prepare and drape the skin as clean as possible, with goal of sterility.
  • Use The appropriately sized chest tube on the affected side
  • The primary landmark for insertion is the 4th or 5th intercostal space in the anterior mid-axillary line. (Note that the risk of hitting the liver or spleen increases if the chest tube is placed more inferiorly, and, a more anteriorly placed chest tube poses a higher risk of injuring the thymus, great vessels, or the heart.
  • The chest tube is angled postero-inferiorly for fluid collections and antero-superiorly in the chest cavity for pneumothorax.
  • An incision is made overlying the skin at the 4th or 5th intercostal space in the anterior mid-axillary line.
  • Using a Kelly or mosquito clamp, blunt dissection is performed directly above the rib through the subcutaneous tissue, avoiding injury to the intercostal neurovascular bundle below the superior rib.
  • Careful, steady pressure is applied to dissect the pleura bluntly. Bracing the clamp with 2 hands while performing this step may help prevent uncontrolled damage to the mediastinal organs.
  • Once inside, the clamp is opened widely to create an entry tract for the chest tube. A rush of air or blood should be noted at this point, depending on the pathology requiring the thoracostostomy.
  • The clamp must be retracted with the prongs open to widen the tract.
  • A finger is inserted inside the tract to sweep the inside of the thoracic cavity and feel for the lung to confirm entry above the abdominal cavity.
  • The chest tube is guided into the thoracic cavity using the Kelly or mosquito clamp.
The last hole on the chest tube should be completely within the thorax.

• Depending on the length, the chest tube may need to be trimmed to ensure the most distal hole is within the chest cavity, especially in small children.
  • Once the chest tube has been properly positioned, it must be secured to the skin , usually with a nonabsorbable suture (eg, silk or nylon).
  • At this point, the chest tube should be connected to the drainage system and wall suction or underwater seal. The indicator on the drainage container should demonstrate that the suction is working properly and set from -10 to -20 mm Hg, depending on physician preference.
  • The quality and quantity of the evacuated liquid or air must be monitored. A chest x-ray must be immediately obtained to confirm that the chest tube is correctly placed.

Post-insertion Dressing Care• Following insertion and suturing to the chest wall, the chest tube should be covered with a nonocclusive dressing. The insertion site must first be covered with Xeroform, followed by gauze and Tegaderm, to create an occlusive dressing. The dressing should remain in place until the chest tube can be removed. Unless it becomes saturated. If warranted, only qualified personnel should change the dressing according to the previously described sequence.
Post-procedure Infection Control• Postprocedure antibiotics are generally not indicated following a chest tube insertion, but their use should be discussed with the attending physician. Infection may be introduced into the chest cavity if the sterile technique is not observed during insertion.
• Dressing changes at the chest tube insertion site must be limited to minimize the introduction of infection.
Collection System Management• Following chest tube insertion, approximately 45 cc of sterile water is added into the atrium via the port located on top of the drain until it reaches the 2 cm fill line. The chest drain is then connected to the patient before initiating suctioning if indicated. Afterward, the suction line is connected to the port on the top of the chest drain atrium.
• The atrium should be kept in an upright position, with the tubing placed below the level of insertion in the chest cavity.
• The chest tube and drainage system must not be stripped. The quality of the output from the chest tube must be checked, with the drainage in the atrium recorded as instructed, no less than every 8 hours per day.
Termination of Chest Tube Treatment• The chest tube should be removed if occluded or no longer needed once clinical or radiographic evidence of improvement is obtained.
• Before chest tube removal, a clamping trial may be indicated to test how the patient responds without the chest tube in place.
• Chest tube clamping trial may be performed by placing a Kelly clamp across the tubing that connects the chest tube to the atrium device. The vital signs should be monitored carefully during a clamping trial.

• A low threshold for removing the Kelly clamp should be used during a clamping trial, ensuring that the patient does not desaturate or exhibit worsening chest pain during this time.
  • At the end of the clamping trial, a chest x-ray image should be obtained to evaluate for worsening pneumothorax or effusion. If the clamping trial is successful, a discussion should be held to determine the timing of chest tube removal.
  • Re-accumulation of pneumothorax or effusion may warrant a longer duration of chest tube therapy.
  • The process is initiated by removing the chest tube dressing and taking the chest tube atrium off-suction. Scissors may be used to remove the suture securing the chest tube to the skin surface. The chest tube must be free from all attachments to the patient.
  • The patients’ respirations must be observed, noting the timing of peak inspiration or expiration on the monitor.
  • The chest tube must be quickly pulled out of the chest cavity once the patient has reached a moment of peak inspiration to prevent pneumothorax.
  • Immediately following chest tube removal, another occlusive dressing is placed on the site using Xeroform, 4 x 4 gauze, and Tegaderm. This dressing must be completely secured and occlusive. Otherwise, air may leak into the wound, accumulate, and cause a tension pneumothorax.
  • A post-removal chest x-ray is indicated to assess for pneumothorax development.
Complications

• Intra-thoracic and intra-abdominal organs injury. In particular, a left-sided chest tube in the neonate carries a high risk of penetrating the pericardium, given these patients' thin chest walls. No differences in mortality have been reported when comparing needle aspiration versus chest tube drainage to manage neonatal pneumothorax.
  • Other potential complications include perforation of the lung, diaphragm, or mediastinum. Importantly, complications may not be readily apparent, as clinical findings are often nonspecific despite thoracic or abdominal organ injury.
  • chest tubes occupying the right superior pleural space and in contact with the phrenic nerve have a higher risk of diaphragm paralysis.
  • premature removal of a chest tube may result in re-accumulation of pleural effusions and may even necessitate reinsertion of a chest tube, thereby increasing hospitalization stay.
  • Dislodgement or disconnection of the Tube: The vital signs should be carefully monitored. If time allows, the chest tube must be cleaned with an alcohol wipe before reconnecting to the drainage system. However, if the patient is acutely decompensating and supplies are not immediately available, the chest tube should be connected to the drainage system, and the attending physician should be notified of the incident. A chest x-ray should be obtained to monitor the patient's condition.
Where is the chest tube usually inserted?
options: 4th or 5th intercostal space, anterior mid-axillary line
read.explanation: Placing it more inferiorly risks the liver or spleen; more anteriorly risks the thymus, great vessels or heart.

read.text:
• A. Indications
    • Lumbar puncture is used to confirm the diagnosis when the baby has signs suggestive of Meningitis.
Contraindications

• spina bifida/meningomylocele
  • Increased intracranial pressure (ICP):
  • Bleeding diathesis: Platelet count greater than 50,000/mm3 is desirable before LP, and correction of any clotting factor deficiencies can minimize the risk for bleeding and subsequent cord or nerve root compression.
  • Overlying skin infection may result in inoculation of CSF with organisms.
  • A mass or evidence of trauma to lumbar vertebrae
  • LP should be deferred in unstable patients, and appropriate therapy should be initiated, including antibiotics, if indicated.
Complications

• Local pain
  • apnea due to positioning
  • Bleeding
  • Infection
  • subarachnoid epidermal cyst
  • epidural CSF leak
  • spinal hematoma, and/or brainstem herniation
Supplies and material needed

• Sterile Gauze
  • Yamidine
  • Plaster
  • Spinal needle or intravenous needle (22- to 24-gauge)
  • Appropriate collection tubes
Preparation

• Be prepared to resuscitate the baby using a bag and mask, if necessary.
  • Place the baby under a radiant warmer, if possible, and undress the baby only when ready to perform the procedure.
  • Position the baby:
      • lateral recumbent position, with hips, knees, and neck flexed. Keep shoulders and hips aligned to avoid rotating the spine.
      • Have the assistant place one hand behind the baby’s head and neck, and place the other hand behind the baby’s thighs to hold the spine in a flexed position
      • Do not compromise a small infant’s cardiorespiratory status with positioning.
  • Locate the desired intervertebral space (either L3 to L4 or L4 to L5) by drawing an imaginary line between the top of the iliac crests. Alternatively, ultrasound can be used to mark the intervertebral space
  • Prepare the skin in a sterile fashion. Place sterile drapes over the baby’s body so that only the puncture site is exposed and .make monitoring the infant possible
  • Overlying skin and interspinous tissue can be anesthetized with 1% lidocaine or Apply local anesthetic cream if sufficient time is available.
PRACTISE THIS SKILL Procedure

• Insert the needle in the midline of the vertebrae, angled towards the baby’s umbilicus.
  • Slowly advance the needle several millimeters at a time, and withdraw stylet frequently to check for CSF flow. Needle may be advanced without the stylet once it is completely through the skin.
  • A slight “pop” may be felt as the needle enters the subarachnoid space. In small infants, one may not feel a change in resistance or “pop”
  • If resistance is met initially and the needle cannot be advanced, withdraw the needle to just under the skin surface and redirect the angle of the needle slightly upward while aiming for the baby’s umbilicus.
  • If CSF still does not come out, remove the needle and reinsert it between the fourth and fifth lumbar processes;
  • If blood is seen in the CSF, the needle probably went through the spinal canal and caused bleeding. If the CSF does not clear, collect enough CSF for culture and sensitivity only.
  • Send CSF for appropriate studies. In general, send the first tube for culture and Gram stain, the second tube for measurement of glucose and protein levels, and the last tube for cell count and differential.
  • After the CSF is collected, remove the needle. Have an assistant apply gentle pressure to the puncture site with a cotton wool ball until bleeding or leakage of fluid stops and apply an adhesive bandage to the site.
Where is a lumbar puncture done in a newborn?
options: L3–L4 or L4–L5, found on the line between the tops of the iliac crests
read.explanation: Baby in the lateral position with hips, knees and neck flexed, without compromising breathing. Tube 1 for culture and Gram stain, tube 2 glucose and protein, last tube cell count.

read.text: Indications:

• To obtain urine for urinalysis and sterile culture
  • to accurately monitor hydration status
  • bladder decompression
Complications:

• Hematuria
  • Infection
  • trauma to urethra or bladder,
  • intravesical knot of catheter (rarely occurs)
Contraindications:

• Pelvic fractures
  • known trauma to the urethra, or blood at the meatus
Catheter selection: :
• 6 Fr for newborns
Preparation :

• Prepare the urethral opening using sterile technique.
  • For collection of urinalysis and/or urine culture, the infant should not have voided within 1 hour of procedure.
PRACTISE THIS SKILL Procedure:

• In males, apply gentle traction to the penis to straighten the urethra.
  • In uncircumcised male infants, expose the meatus with gentle retraction of the foreskin. The foreskin must be retracted only far enough to visualize the meatus.
  • In females, the urethral orifice may be difficult to visualize but is usually immediately superoanterior to the vaginal orifice.
  • Gently insert a lubricated catheter into the urethra. Slowly advance catheter until resistance is met at the external sphincter. Continued pressure will overcome this resistance, and the catheter will enter the bladder. Only a few centimeters of advancement are required to reach the bladder in females. In males, insert a few centimeters longer than the shaft of the penis.
  • Carefully remove the catheter once specimen is obtained, and cleanse skin of iodine.
  • If indwelling Foley catheter is inserted, inflate balloon with sterile water or saline as indicated on bulb, then connect catheter to drainage tubing attached to urine drainage bag. Secure catheter tubing to inner thigh.
What catheter size is used for a newborn's urinary catheterization?
read.explanation: For urine culture, the baby should not have voided within 1 hour.

read.text: Indications:

• To obtain urine in a sterile manner for urinalysis and culture
  • Bladder decompression.
Contraindication

• Neonate with genitourinary track anomalies
  • Coagulopathy
  • intestinal obstruction
Complications:

• Infection (cellulitis)
  • hematuria (usually microscopic),
  • intestinal perforation preparation:
  • Prepare suprapupic area in a sterile fashion.
  • Child should not have voided within 1 hour of procedure.
PRACTISE THIS SKILL Procedure:

• Determine the site for puncture : 1 to 2 cm above the symphysis pubis in the midline
  • Anterior rectal pressure in females or gentle penile pressure in males may be used to prevent urination during the procedure. Restrain child in the supine, frog leg position.
  • Use a syringe with a 22-gauge, 1.5-inch needle, and puncture at a 10- to 20-degree angle to the perpendicular, aiming slightly caudad.
  • Gently exert suction as the needle is advanced until urine enters syringe. The needle should not be advanced more than 3 cm.
  • Aspirate urine with gentle suction.
  • Remove needle, cleanse skin of iodine, and apply a sterile bandage.
Where is suprapubic aspiration done?
options: 1–2 cm above the symphysis pubis in the midline
read.explanation: A 22-gauge 1.5-inch needle, 10–20 degrees from the perpendicular, aiming slightly caudad, not more than 3 cm deep.

Parts of a radiant warmer

Standard operating Procedure for warmer

• 1. Turn on the warmer 20 min before put baby to pre warm the linen and mattress.
  • 2. Ensure the mattress and linen are clean.
  • 3. Select the mode
      • Manual mode: Heater output increased or decreased manually, Used for initial preparation of bed and for rapid warming of a severely hypothermic baby, Respond to alarm immediately. Identify the fault and rectify it

  • 4. Set the target temperature to 36.5 – 37.0 °C.
  • 5. Apply probe over the right hypochondrium in supine position and in flank in prone position
  • 6. Connect skin probe to the baby’s abdomen with sticking tape.
      • Check sensor probe regularly to ensure it is in place every 2-3hours
      • Check and record the temperature every 2-3 hours and record
      • Change probe site once in every 24 hours

Standard operating Procedure of Infant Incubator

• 1. Ensure the Incubator clean and disinfected before use
  • 2. Connect the device to a reliable power source and ensure the power cable is intact.
  • 3. Switch on the incubator using the main power button.
  • 4. Select Mode
      • a. Servo Mode (skin control): Set the temperature to 36.5–37°C.
      • b. Manual Mode (Air Mode): set temperature as follow
          • i. Extremely preterm (<28 wks.): 34–36°C
          • ii. Very preterm (28–32 wks.): 33–34°C
          • iii. Near-term/term: 32–33°C
  • 5. Attach the skin temperature probe to the abdomen or back
      • a. Change probe site every 8–12 hours
  • 6. Ensure water reservoir filled with sterile or distilled water
  • 7. Adjust humidity
      • a. Start usually between 40–70% depending on the infant’s weight and condition. Except ELBW/VLBW (<1500g) → 70–90% in first week
      • b. After 1 week → Gradually reduce to 40–50%
  • 8. Place the infant inside and close all access doors securely.
  • 9. Monitor axillary temperature at least 2–4 times/day.
  • 10. Minimize opening portholes (prevents heat/humidity loss
Infant Incubator Disinfection

• 1. Incubators should be cleaned at least every week or Between Patients
  • 2. disinfect Frequent touch points e.g., door handles and latches 3 times per day
  • 3. Disinfect Hood (external surface) and IV pole daily
  • 4. Disinfect Water reservoir, Mattress, Inner double wall weekly
  • 5. Change water reservoir for humidification daily with distill water

PRACTISE THIS SKILL Steps for terminal Disinfection (weekly or between patient)
• 1. Perform hand hygiene and wear the appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE).
Always wear clean gloves. Sterile gloves are not necessary.

• 2. Disassemble the incubator for optimum cleaning and disinfection.
  • 3. Wipe off and remove all accumulated fluids and soiling and debris by wiping with a dampened cloth. Use a soft and neutral detergent like soap if necessary
  • 4. Wipe with a disinfectant three times and put parts in disinfection solution for 20 minutes.
  • 5. Wipe with a wet cloth to remove residual disinfectant.
  • 6. Ensure that clean water is used.
  • 7. Ensure that all holes and indentations are cleaned.
  • 8. Wait for the product to air dry for 45 minutes.
  • 9. If incubators are recurrently positive for microorganisms, especially Pseudomonas-like bacteria, the water source may be contaminated. To decontaminate, it is suggested to pour 250ml of 24% acetic acid once weekly for 10 weeks into sink drains and wait for 30 minutes before flushing

Standard Operating Procedure of Vayu CPAP

• Ensure all component are clean and disinfected
  • Assemble the system according to manufacturer guidance, ensure correct connections.
  • Monitor Devices
      • Refill humidifier before water drops below the “REFILL” line
      • Refill pressure generator when water drops below “fill mark”
      • Replace water in jars every 24 hours
      • Replace filter disk Every 24 hours, replace Earlier if discolored or after each patient
  • Ensure continuous bubbling at all times
  • Monitor Patient
      • Continuous assessment of: Work of breathing, Oxygen saturation, Heart rate
      • Adjust pressure based on clinical response
  • Confirm oxygen cylinder pressure regularly
Vayu CPAP Disinfection

• 1. Empty the jars, remove any gross soiling then fully disassemble the device
  • 2. Soak in clean water until ready to reprocess
  • 3. Clean with enzymatic detergent or dish soap, Use a soft-bristled brush or sponge
  • 4. Brush lumens AND Flush lumens 3 times
  • 5. Rinse all components
  • 6. High-level Disinfection
      • flushing each lumen with disinfectant at least 3 times.
      • fully immerse all components in the disinfectant, making sure all lumens are completely filled.
      • Use 0.5% chlorine solution (soak for 10 min) or 2.5%-3.5% glutaraldehyde (soak for 40 min)
      • Do not autoclave, boil, steam sterilize
      • Rinse AND flush lumens 3 times with high volumes of water to remove disinfectant residues
  • 7. Air dry or wipe dry with gauze
  • 8. Store the device in its pre-assembled form in a clean container out of direct sunlight

read.text: It is a simple, non-invasive and portable method to monitor oxygen saturation and heart rate with good accuracy.

Situations in which pulse-oximetry does not work

• Hypovolemic states or low perfusion states

Standard operating Procedure

• Hand Hygiene

  • Switch on the pulse oximeter

  • Ensure both the sides of probe are directly opposite each other
  • Secure probe in place
  • Set high and low alarms limits for saturation and heart rate.
  • Observer and change site every 6-8 hourly (If applied continuously)
  • After use switch it off.
  • Clean the probe with spirit and keep covered if not required for any baby.
Clean/Disinfect
• Clean with spirit swab and let it dry before and after any using.

  • STOP INFUSION
  • Press [STOP] button to stop infusion during the operation.
  • Before restart infusion, FLOW RATE, DELIVERY VOLUME, the amount of solution volume should be confirmed.
Infusion Pump Disinfection

• Before cleaning the pump, make sure to power off the pump and disconnect the AC power cord.
  • Do not immerse the pump in water.
  • Do not immerse the pump in any liquid nor allow any liquid to leak into the pump.
  • Do not use alcohol, thinner, benzene, ammonia, acetone or any other organic solvents.
  • Do not sterilize the pump.
  • When the pump casing is stained, use a gauze cloth or similar, moistened with cold or tepid water and let it dry, especially the AC power inlet before use.
  • When the Air-In-Line detector or Occlusion detector is stained, use a swab moistened with warm water and let it dry before use.
  • Do not use something rigid or sharp like tweezers to clean the detectors
  • Before cleaning the drop sensor, make sure to disconnect the drop sensor completely from the pump.
  • When the drop sensor is stained, use a gauze cloth or similar, moistened with cold or tepid water and let it dry.
  • Do not allow any solution to splash on the drip sensor connector. If it is wetted, dry it before use.
How is the infusion pump cleaned?
options: Power off, unplug, and wipe with gauze moistened with cold or tepid water; never immerse it or use alcohol or solvents

read.text: Standard operation Procedure

• Connect to the mains Switch on the unit and occlude distal end with your thumb to check the suction pressure.
  • Position a conscious patient in the semi- fowler’s position with the head turned to one side for oral suctioning or with the neck hyper extended for nasal suctioning.
  • Position the unconscious patient in the lateral position facing the nurse.
  • Do a non-sterile glove on the non-dominant hand and then a sterile glove on the other hand, attach the catheter to suction unit.
  • Use disposable suction catheters
  • Connect the desired size disposable suction catheter to the suctioning tubing
      • Preterm baby size 4-5 Fr
      • Neonate- birth- 28 days 6Fr
  • Ensure the negative pressure does not exceed 100 mm of Hg
  • For all suctioning episodes the lowest negative pressure should be used for suctioning, with the smallest catheter and the shortest suctioning time
  • Perform suction gently by inserting only 5 cm in mouth and apply pressure while withdrawing.
  • Suction only intermittently, Limit suction time to 10-15 seconds.
  • Discontinue if heart rate decreases by 20 beats/minute or increase by 40 beats/minute or if any cardiac ectopy is observed.
  • Rinse catheter between suctioning.
  • Continue doing suction until the airway are clean of accumulated secretions but no more than 4 suctioning be made per episode
Cleaning and disinfection of Suction Machin

• Disconnect the suction catheter tip from the suction tubing and discard appropriately
  • Change suction catheter between patient and patient
  • Disinfect the suction pump pressure gauge controls using gauze and 70% alcohol.
  • Disinfect collection reservoir after each patient
      • a. Remove the collection reservoir from suction pump and dispose of contents.
      • b. Wash with detergent from any visible dirt
      • c. soak the bottle in Chlorine solution or 2% glutaraldehyde solution for 20 min
      • d. Take out from disinfection solution and wash under running water
  • Disinfect collection reservoir after each patient
      • a. Remove the tube from suction pump.
      • b. Wash by Flush the suction tubing by suctioning with clean water
      • c. soak the bottle in Chlorine solution or 2% glutaraldehyde solution for 20 min
      • d. Flush the suction tubing by suctioning with clean water after each use.
Suctioning a newborn: what is the maximum negative pressure, and for how long?
options: Not over 100 mm Hg; 10–15 seconds at a time
read.explanation: Preterm catheter 4–5 Fr; neonate 6 Fr; insert only 5 cm in the mouth. Stop if the heart rate falls by 20 or rises by 40, or with ectopy. No more than 4 suctions per episode.

read.text: A reusable, hand-held, manual suction device designed to suck gently and clear excessive mucus from the airway of a newborn to facilitate easier breathing. The life span of the device is minimum 3 years or 20 autoclave sessions, whichever comes first. Standard procedure

• 1. Always use clean disinfected Bulb
  • 2. squeeze the air out of the bulb. Keep the bulb squeezed.
  • 3. Gently place the tip of the squeezed bulb into a nostril.

• 4. Let go of the bulb to let the air back into it. This will pull the mucus out of the nose and into the bulb.
    • 5. Squeeze the mucus out of the bulb and onto a tissue.
    • 6. Suction the other nostril the same way.
    • 7. If mucus is too thick to suction, you can thin it with saline
  • 8. Gently wipe off the mucus around the baby’s nose with tissues to prevent irritation.
Disinfection of The Suction Bulb

• Wash the bulb syringe in warm, soapy water after each use.
  • Squeeze soapy water into the bulb and shake to clean out the mucus. Then, squeeze the water out.
  • Put in chlorine solution foe 20 minutes
  • Rinse the bulb many times by filling it with clear water, then squeezing the water out.
  • Also, can be autoclaved at 136°C
Using a suction bulb on a newborn: what is the first step at the nose?
options: Squeeze the air out of the bulb first, then place the tip gently in the nostril and let go
Put the tip in, then squeeze
Use it on the mouth only
read.explanation: Then squeeze the mucus out onto a tissue and do the other nostril. Wash in soapy water, then chlorine for 20 minutes.

read.text:
• Fit the mask over the nose and mouth. Press firmly to prevent air leaks.
  • Hold with the thumb on one side and the index and middle fingers on the other.
  • With the other hand, squeeze the bag at a rate of 30 to 60 breaths/minute for 60 seconds. Ventilation is effective if the chest rises and falls.
IMPORTANT

• excessive ventilation pressure can cause a pneumothorax.
    • If the chest fails to rise:
        • Check the connection between the bag and the mask.
        • Correct the position of the mask on the face.
        • Correct the head position.
    • Check every minute for spontaneous respiratory effort (look for chest movement); do not take the mask off the neonate’s face to check for spontaneous breathing.
    • Continue manual ventilation until there is spontaneous respiratory effort.
Bag and Mask Disinfection

• Rinse the components under running (tap) water to remove gross soil.
  • soak the device in in soupy solution, for the removal of residues of dried blood with using a soft brush until all visible soil is removed.
  • Rinse the components with running (tap) water for one minute.
  • Fully immerse the device in disinfection solution for the 20 minutes
  • Rinse the device by fully immersing it in distill water and repeat for a total of 3 rinses using a fresh batch of distill water each time.
  • Dry the device using a sterile cloth.
  • Autoclave can be used with running a full cycle at 134 – 135 °C with an exposure time of 10 minutes and a dry time of 45 minutes.
Bag and mask ventilation: what rate, and how do you know it is effective?
options: 30–60 breaths a minute; the chest rises and falls
100 breaths a minute; the baby cries
10 breaths a minute; the bag empties
read.explanation: If the chest does not rise: check the bag–mask connection, the mask position and the head position. Excessive pressure can cause a pneumothorax.

read.text: Oxygen concentrators are machines that extract nitrogen from atmospheric air, resulting in an output of almost pure oxygen.
Position the concentrator so that it is at least 30 cm away from walls or curtains, so that the inlet at the back is not obstructed.
Plug the power cord into the mains electricity supply
Turn on the concentrator (switch on the console). A green light should come on when a sufficiently high oxygen concentration is reached, usually within 10 min
Adjust the flow meter to the flow required for the patient or, if using a flow splitter, the number of patients receiving oxygen.
Disinfection
Concentrators have a large particulate filter over the air inlet (usually at the back of freestanding or portable models) to stop dust and other airborne particles from entering the unit.
The filter should be removed and cleaned in warm soapy water, dried with an absorbent towel and replaced.
The exterior of the oxygen concentrator should be cleaned with a mild disinfecting cleaning agent or a diluted solution of bleach (5.25% sodium hypochlorite)
Allow the solution to remain on the surface for 10 min, and then rinse off and dry.
How far from walls or curtains is an oxygen concentrator placed?
options: At least 30 cm, so the air inlet is not blocked
read.explanation: A green light shows when a high enough oxygen concentration is reached, usually within 10 minutes. Clean the inlet filter in warm soapy water.
